prompt:
Let $G$ be a group of order $2^4\cdot5^3\cdot11$ and let $H$ be a group of order $5^3\cdot11$.

(a) Show that $H$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup.

(b) If the number of Sylow $5$-subgroups of $G$ is (strictly) less than $16$, prove that $G$ has a proper normal subgroup of order divisible by $5$.

(c) If $G$ has exactly sixteen Sylow $5$-subgroups, show that $G$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup.
answer: (a) $n_{11}(H)\mid125$, $\equiv1\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}=1$. (b) $n_5\in\{1,11\}$; for $11$, the kernel of the action on the $11$ cosets of $N_G(P)$ is proper and has order divisible by $5$ since $5^3\nmid11!$. (c) $N_G(P)$ has order $5^3\cdot11$, so by (a) contains a normal Sylow 11-subgroup $Q$; $n_{11}(G)\mid16$ and $\equiv1\pmod{11}$, so $Q\trianglelefteq G$.

solutions.title: Sylow counting and permutation action
solutions.body:
$|G|=2^4\cdot5^3\cdot11=22000$.

**(a)** $n_{11}(H)$ divides $5^3$ and is $\equiv1\pmod{11}$. The divisors $1,5,25,125$ are $\equiv1,5,3,4\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}(H)=1$.

**(b)** $n_5=n_5(G)$ divides $2^4\cdot11=176$ and $n_5\equiv1\pmod5$. The divisors of $176$ below $16$ are $1,2,4,8,11$, of which $1$ and $11$ are $\equiv1\pmod5$. If $n_5=1$, the Sylow $5$-subgroup is normal, proper, of order $125$. If $n_5=11$, let $N=N_G(P)$ for $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_5(G)$, so $|G:N|=11$. $G$ acts on the $11$ right cosets of $N$, giving $\theta\colon G\to S_{11}$ with kernel $K\subseteq N$; in particular $K\ne G$. Since $G/K$ embeds in $S_{11}$ and $5^3\nmid11!$ (the $5$-part of $11!$ is $5^2$), $5\mid|K|$. So $K$ is the required proper normal subgroup.

**(c)** If $n_5=16$, let $N=N_G(P)$; then $|N|=22000/16=1375=5^3\cdot11$. By (a), $N$ has a normal Sylow $11$-subgroup $Q$, which is also a Sylow $11$-subgroup of $G$. Since $N\subseteq N_G(Q)$, $n_{11}(G)=|G:N_G(Q)|$ divides $|G:N|=16$. The divisors $1,2,4,8,16$ are $\equiv1,2,4,8,5\pmod{11}$, so $n_{11}(G)=1$ and $Q\trianglelefteq G$. ∎

prompt:
Let $L/K$ be a finite degree Galois extension of fields with Galois group given by $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)=G$, and let $E$ be an intermediate field. Then $E$ is said to be a *2-tower* over $K$ if there exists a chain of fields $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$ such that $|E_i:E_{i-1}|=2$ for all $i=1,2,\ldots,n$.

(a) If $G$ is abelian, prove that $E$ is a 2-tower over $K$ if and only if the degree $|E:K|$ is a power of $2$.

(b) Show by example that the characterization of 2-towers given in part (a) is false if $G$ is allowed to be a nonabelian group.
answer: (a) A tower has degree $2^n$; conversely $E/K$ is Galois with abelian group of order $2^n$, which has a chain of subgroups of index $2$. (b) For a quartic with Galois group $A_4$, e.g. $x^4+8x+12$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, $E=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$ ($\theta$ a root) has degree $4$, but $A_4$ has no subgroup of order 6 between $A_3$ and $A_4$, so no intermediate quadratic field.

solutions.title: Galois correspondence
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $E$ is a 2-tower, $|E:K|=\prod|E_i:E_{i-1}|=2^n$. Conversely, let $|E:K|=2^n$. By the Galois correspondence $E=L^H$ for some $H\le G$; $G$ abelian implies $H\trianglelefteq G$, so $E/K$ is Galois with group $A=G/H$, an abelian group of order $2^n$. A finite abelian (indeed any) $2$-group has a chain $A=A_0\supseteq A_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq A_n=1$ with $|A_{i-1}:A_i|=2$ (e.g. a composition series). Put $E_i=E^{A_i}$. Then $K=E_0\subseteq E_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq E_n=E$ and $|E_i:E_{i-1}|=|A_{i-1}:A_i|=2$. So $E$ is a 2-tower.

**(b)** We need a Galois extension with group $A_4$ and an intermediate field of degree $4$ with no intermediate quadratic field. Let $f=x^4+8x+12\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and $L$ its splitting field.
- $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$: it has no rational root (none of $\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\pm4,\pm6,\pm12$ is a root, as $f>0$ for $x\ge0$ and one checks the negative ones), and by Gauss's lemma a factorization into quadratics would be $(x^2+ax+b)(x^2-ax+c)$ with integers satisfying $b+c=a^2$, $a(c-b)=8$, $bc=12$; for $a\in\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4,\pm8\}$ the first two equations give $(b,c)$ non-integral or equal to $(0,4),(4,0),(7,9),(9,7)$, none with $bc=12$.
- Its discriminant is $-27\cdot8^4+256\cdot12^3=331776=576^2$, a square, so $G\le A_4$.
- Its resolvent cubic $x^3-48x-64$ has no rational root (test the divisors of $64$), so it is irreducible and $3\mid|G|$, while $4\mid|G|$ since $f$ is irreducible.

Hence $|G|=12$ and $G=A_4$. Let $\theta$ be a root of $f$ and $E=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, so $|E:\mathbb{Q}|=4=2^2$, and $E=L^H$ where $H$ is the stabilizer of $\theta$, of order $3$. If $E$ were a 2-tower, there would be $E_1$ with $|E_1:\mathbb{Q}|=2$, $\mathbb{Q}\subset E_1\subset E$, corresponding to a subgroup $T$ with $H<T<A_4$ and $|T|=6$. But $A_4$ has no subgroup of order $6$. So $E$ is not a 2-tower although its degree is a power of $2$.

(The official example is the same in spirit: $A_4$ acting on $L=F(x_1,\dots,x_4)$ by permuting variables, $K=L^{A_4}$, $E=L^{A_3}$; $A_3$ is a maximal subgroup of $A_4$.) ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix over the complex numbers and assume that the rank of $A$ is equal to $1$.

(a) What are the possible Jordan canonical forms for $A$? Justify your answer.

(b) For each of the forms obtained in part (a), compute the characteristic polynomial of $A$ and the minimal polynomial of $A$.
answer: (a) Either $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$ with $\lambda=\mathrm{tr}\,A\neq0$, or (when $\mathrm{tr}\,A=0$, $n\ge2$) one block $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ plus zeros. (b) First case: $\chi=x^{n-1}(x-\lambda)$, $m=x(x-\lambda)$. Second case: $\chi=x^n$, $m=x^2$.

solutions.title: Rank of Jordan blocks
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $B$ be the Jordan form of $A$; $\mathrm{rank}\,B=\mathrm{rank}\,A=1$. The rank of a block diagonal matrix is the sum of the ranks of the blocks. A Jordan block $J_k(\mu)$ has rank $k$ if $\mu\ne0$ and rank $k-1$ if $\mu=0$. So exactly one block has rank $1$ and all others have rank $0$, i.e. are $J_1(0)=(0)$. The rank-1 block is either $J_1(\lambda)=(\lambda)$ with $\lambda\ne0$, or $J_2(0)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Hence
$$B=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)\ (\lambda\ne0)\qquad\text{or}\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus0_{n-2}\ (n\ge2).$$
In both cases $\lambda=\mathrm{tr}\,B=\mathrm{tr}\,A$, so the first occurs iff $\mathrm{tr}\,A\ne0$. Both occur (e.g. $E_{11}$ and $E_{12}$).

**(b)** Similar matrices have the same characteristic and minimal polynomials.
- $B=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda,0,\dots,0)$, $\lambda\ne0$: $\chi_A=x^{n-1}(x-\lambda)$; $B$ is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda\neq0$ and (if $n\ge2$) $0$, so $m_A=x(x-\lambda)$ for $n\ge2$ (and $m_A=x-\lambda$ when $n=1$).
- $B=J_2(0)\oplus0$: $\chi_A=x^n$, and $m_A=x^2$ (the largest Jordan block has size $2$). ∎

prompt:
Let $R=F[x,y]$ be the polynomial ring over the field $F$ in the two indeterminates $x$ and $y$, and let $I=xR$ be the principal ideal of $R$ generated by $x$. Define $S=F+I$, so that $S$ is a subring of $R$, and observe that $I$ is an ideal of $S$.

(a) Show that $I$ is not finitely generated as an ideal of $S$.

(b) Prove that there are infinitely many ideals of $S$ that are not ideals of $R$.
answer: (a) If $I=a_1S+\cdots+a_kS$, then modulo $I^2=x^2R$ every element of $I$ is an $F$-combination of the $a_i$, so $xy^n$ with $n$ above all $y$-degrees is not reached. (b) The principal $S$-ideals $xy^nS=Fxy^n+x^2y^nR$ ($n\ge0$) are pairwise distinct and none is an $R$-ideal, as $xy^{n+1}\notin xy^nS$. (Alternatively: a strictly ascending chain of $S$-ideals can contain only finitely many $R$-ideals, $R$ being Noetherian.)

solutions.title: Work modulo $x^2$
solutions.body:
**(a)** Suppose $I=a_1S+\cdots+a_kS$ with $a_i\in I=xF[x,y]$. Let $n$ exceed the $y$-degrees of all $a_i$. Then $xy^n\in I$, so
$$xy^n=\sum_ia_i(f_i+b_i),\qquad f_i\in F,\ b_i\in I.$$
Each $a_ib_i\in I^2=x^2R$, so all its monomials are divisible by $x^2$. Hence the terms of $xy^n$ that are not divisible by $x^2$ must come from $\sum f_ia_i$, a polynomial of $y$-degree $<n$. But $xy^n$ is itself not divisible by $x^2$ and has $y$-degree $n$, a contradiction. So $I$ is not finitely generated over $S$.

**(b)** *Argument 1 (Noetherian).* By (a), $S$ is not Noetherian, so there is a strictly ascending chain $J_1\subsetneq J_2\subsetneq\cdots$ of ideals of $S$. $R$ is Noetherian (Hilbert basis theorem). If infinitely many $J_i$ were ideals of $R$, they would form a strictly ascending chain of ideals of $R$, impossible. So all but finitely many $J_i$ are ideals of $S$ that are not ideals of $R$; these are infinitely many distinct ideals.

*Argument 2 (explicit).* For $n\ge0$ let $J_n=xy^nS=Fxy^n+x^2y^nR$, an ideal of $S$. These are distinct for different $n$: the elements of $J_n$ not divisible by $x^2$ have $x$-linear part exactly $c\,xy^n$ with $c\ne0$. And $J_n$ is not an ideal of $R$: $y\cdot xy^n=xy^{n+1}\notin J_n$, since its $x$-linear part is $xy^{n+1}$, not a scalar multiple of $xy^n$. ∎
